question: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & x & y\\x & 1 & z\\y & z & 1\end{bmatrix}$. For which real values of $x$, $y$, $z$ is $A$ both symmetric and invertible? Analyze and justify. If $A$ is not invertible for certain values, determine those values and interpret the result.
explanation:
$A$ is symmetric for all $x, y, z$.

Invertibility: Compute $|A|$. Expanding along row 1:

$|A| = 1\cdot\begin{vmatrix}1 & z\\z & 1\end{vmatrix} - x\cdot\begin{vmatrix}x & z\\y & 1\end{vmatrix} + y\cdot\begin{vmatrix}x & 1\\y & z\end{vmatrix}$

$= 1(1 - z^2) - x(x - y z) + y(x z - y)$

$= (1-z^2) - (x^2 - x y z) + (x y z - y^2)$

$= 1 - z^2 - x^2 + x y z + x y z - y^2$

$= 1 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2 + 2 x y z$

So $A$ is invertible (i.e., $|A| \ne 0$) iff $1 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2 + 2 x y z \ne 0$.

It is non-invertible if $1 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2 + 2 x y z = 0$. This is the set of all real solutions to this equation, which geometrically forms a surface in $\mathbb{R}^3$. If any $x, y, z$ satisfy this, the corresponding $A$ is not invertible and the linear system it would define is dependent.

options.A: $A$ is symmetric for all real $x,y,z$. It is invertible iff $1-x^2-y^2-z^2+2xyz\ne0$. It is non-invertible iff $1-x^2-y^2-z^2+2xyz=0$.
options.B: $A$ is symmetric only when $x=y=z=0$, and it is invertible only when $x+y+z=0$.
options.C: $A$ is always invertible because all diagonal entries are $1$.
options.D: $A$ is non-invertible for all real $x,y,z$ because it is symmetric.
